Cautiously accommodative tone. The Committee’s 25 bp rate cut to 1.50–1.75% amid “muted inflation pressures” aligns with rules-based guidance and New Keynesian evidence that expected inflation and the output gap drive inflation dynamics (Taylor, 1983; Galí, Gertler, and López-Salido). The emphasis on weak business fixed investment and exports is macro-relevant: investment shortfalls, including inventory investment, are tightly linked to internal finance and credit conditions and have historically accounted for notable portions of declines in real GDP (Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein, 1994; investment–GDP linkages in standard texts). The Desk’s T-bill purchases and repo operations to maintain “ample reserves” support transmission via the liquidity effect and help avoid money-market frictions that could impair policy implementation (B. Friedman; Sims, 1992 on real effects of monetary shocks). With market-based inflation compensation low but survey expectations little changed, maintaining accommodation is consistent with stabilizing expectations while supporting activity (Cagan, 1956; McCallum and Nelson, 1999). Two dissents favoring no cut underscore uncertainty, but the overall stance aims to sustain expansion with inflation moving toward the symmetric 2% objective. Net sentiment: slightly positive, tempered by investment weakness and soft inflation.
